claim: Bacterial leaf blight (BB) of rice is caused by Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae (Xoo).
source: Bacterial leaf blight (BB) of rice, caused by Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae (Xoo), threatens global food security and the livelihood of small-scale rice producers.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the causative agent of bacterial leaf blight in rice.

claim: Analyses of Xoo collections from Asia, Africa and the Americas demonstrated complete continental segregation.
source: Analyses of Xoo collections from Asia, Africa and the Americas demonstrated complete continental segregation, despite robust global rice trade.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous analyses showing phylogenetic separation of Xoo strains by continent.

claim: Unprecedented BB outbreaks occurred in Tanzania.
source: Here, we report unprecedented BB outbreaks in Tanzania.
evidence: The manuscript reports new field observations and disease surveys in Tanzania.

claim: The causative strains in Tanzania carry Asian-type TAL effectors targeting the sucrose transporter SWEET11a.
source: The causative strains, unlike endemic African Xoo, carry Asian-type TAL effectors targeting the sucrose transporter SWEET11a and iTALes suppressing Xa1.
evidence: The manuscript presents genomic sequencing and functional data showing the presence of Asian-type TAL effectors.

claim: The causative strains in Tanzania carry iTALes suppressing Xa1.
source: The causative strains, unlike endemic African Xoo, carry Asian-type TAL effectors targeting the sucrose transporter SWEET11a and iTALes suppressing Xa1.
evidence: The manuscript presents genomic sequencing data showing the presence of iTALes.

claim: Phylogenomics clustered the Tanzanian strains with Xoo from Southern-China.
source: Phylogenomics clustered these strains with Xoo from Southern-China.
evidence: The manuscript presents phylogenetic analysis based on whole genome SNP data.

claim: African rice varieties do not carry effective resistance against the newly introduced Tanzanian strains.
source: African rice varieties do not carry effective resistance.
evidence: The manuscript presents infection assays showing susceptibility of African varieties to the new strains.

claim: A hybrid CRISPR-Cas9/Cpf1 system was developed to edit all known TALe-binding elements in three SWEET promoters of the East African elite variety Komboka.
source: To protect African rice production against this emerging threat, we developed a hybrid CRISPR-Cas9/Cpf1 system to edit all known TALe-binding elements in three SWEET promoters of the East African elite variety Komboka.
evidence: The manuscript describes the construction and application of the genome editing system.

claim: The edited Komboka lines show broad-spectrum resistance against Asian and African strains of Xoo.
source: The edited lines show broad-spectrum resistance against Asian and African strains of Xoo, including strains recently discovered in Tanzania.
evidence: The manuscript presents infection assays showing resistance of edited lines to multiple Xoo strains.

claim: The edited Komboka lines show resistance against strains recently discovered in Tanzania.
source: The edited lines show broad-spectrum resistance against Asian and African strains of Xoo, including strains recently discovered in Tanzania.
evidence: The manuscript presents infection assays showing resistance of edited lines to Tanzanian strains.

claim: Rice is one of the most important staple foods for developing countries in Asia and Africa.
source: Rice is one of the most important staple foods for developing countries in Asia and Africa (Odongo et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Odongo et al., 2021.

claim: African consumers increasingly replace traditional staples such as sorghum, millet, and maize with rice.
source: African consumers increasingly replace traditional staples such as sorghum, millet, and maize with rice.
evidence: This is a statement about dietary trends in Africa.

claim: African farmers produce ~60% of local rice demand.
source: Today, African farmers, 90% of which are small-scale food producers with <1 ha of land (Pandey et al., 2010), produce ~60% of local rice demand.
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about rice production in Africa, supported by a citation.

claim: 90% of African farmers are small-scale food producers with <1 ha of land.
source: Today, African farmers, 90% of which are small-scale food producers with <1 ha of land (Pandey et al., 2010), produce ~60% of local rice demand.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pandey et al., 2010.

claim: The African population is expected to double until 2050.
source: The demand will likely increase with the expected doubling of the population until 2050.
evidence: This is a demographic projection.

claim: Productivity in African rice farming is often hampered by diseases, such as Bacterial Leaf Blight (BB), Rice Yellow Mottle Virus (RYMV), and Rice Blast (RB).
source: Productivity is often hampered by diseases, such as Bacterial Leaf Blight (BB), Rice Yellow Mottle Virus (RYMV), and Rice Blast (RB) (Jiang et al., 2020; Longue et al., 2018; Mutiga et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: BB is caused by the bacterium Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae (Xoo).
source: BB, caused by the bacterium Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae (Xoo), is a devastating rice disease in many rice-growing countries.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge.

claim: Xoo comprises a wide spectrum of pathovars with diverse virulence mechanisms.
source: Xoo comprises a wide spectrum of pathovars with diverse virulence mechanisms.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Xoo diversity.

claim: Resistance (R) genes for BB have been identified in rice.
source: In rice, resistance (R) genes for BB have been identified and are used extensively to breed resistant varieties.
evidence: This is established knowledge about rice breeding.

claim: Resistance based on single R genes was rapidly overcome by new pathovars.
source: However, resistance based on single R genes was rapidly overcome by new pathovars (Vera Cruz et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vera Cruz et al., 2000.

claim: Regular monitoring of the virulence of current Xoo populations has provided effective guidance for stacking different R genes to obtain broad-spectrum resistance in Asian rice varieties.
source: Regular monitoring of the virulence of current Xoo populations on a collection of rice tester lines carrying single or combinations of R genes has provided effective guidance for stacking different R genes to obtain broad-spectrum resistance in Asian rice varieties (Arra et al., 2017; Arra et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Arra et al., 2017 and 2018.

claim: BB was first reported in Mali and Cameroon in the late 1970s in Africa.
source: In Africa, BB was first reported in Mali and Cameroon in the late 1970s, and later in several other West African countries (Buddenhagen et al., 1979; Verdier et al., 2012b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Buddenhagen et al., 1979 and Verdier et al., 2012b.

claim: East African countries recently reported BB epidemics.
source: Recently, East African countries also reported BB epidemics (Duku et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Duku et al., 2016.

claim: BB is not yet considered a major threat in Africa.
source: While information on the spread and severity of BB in Africa is scarce, BB is not yet considered a major threat in Africa; nevertheless, BB is an established disease.
evidence: This is a statement about the current perception of BB threat in Africa.

claim: Climate change affects BB disease spread in Africa.
source: The situation is unstable, because climate change affects disease spread, and damage is expected to become more severe in the future due to climate change (Amos, 2013; Laha et al., 2016; Sere and Ouedraogo, 2005; Verdier et al., 2012b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Xoo strains secrete a suite of Transcription Activator-Like effectors (TALes) into rice xylem parenchyma cells via type III secretion systems.
source: Xoo strains secrete a suite of Transcription Activator-Like effectors (TALes) into rice xylem parenchyma cells via type III secretion systems.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Xoo virulence mechanisms.

claim: TALes are targeted to the nucleus once inside the host cell.
source: Once inside the host cell, TALes are targeted to the nucleus, where they bind to effector binding elements (EBEs) in the promoters of specific host genes via a unique domain of tandemly arranged 34 amino-acid long repeats.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TALe function.

claim: TALes bind to effector binding elements (EBEs) in the promoters of specific host genes via a unique domain of tandemly arranged 34 amino-acid long repeats.
source: Once inside the host cell, TALes are targeted to the nucleus, where they bind to effector binding elements (EBEs) in the promoters of specific host genes via a unique domain of tandemly arranged 34 amino-acid long repeats.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TALe-DNA binding.

claim: TALes function as transcriptional activators that trigger ectopic induction of target genes.
source: TALes function as transcriptional activators that trigger ectopic induction of target genes (Richter et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Richter et al., 2014.

claim: Several Xoo TALes induce one or several host SWEET sucrose uniporter genes (SWEET11a, 13 and 14).
source: Several Xoo TALes induce one or several host SWEET sucrose uniporter genes (SWEET11a, 13 and 14), presumably causing sucrose release from the xylem parenchyma into the apoplasm at the sites where the bacteria reside and reproduce (note that due to the discovery of a previously misannotated sucrose transporting paralog, SWEET11a was renamed formerly SWEET11 Wu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge about TALe targets, with a citation to Wu et al., 2022 for nomenclature.

claim: Sucrose is consumed by the bacteria, resulting in effective reproduction.
source: Sucrose is consumed by the bacteria, resulting in effective reproduction (Sadoine et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sadoine et al., 2021.

claim: Six target EBEs in SWEET promoters have been identified in a comprehensive Xoo collection.
source: To date, six target EBEs in SWEET promoters have been identified in a comprehensive Xoo collection.
evidence: This is a summary of previous research findings.

claim: Asian and African Xoo strains are phylogenetically distinct and use distinct TALes to target SWEETs.
source: Notably, Asian and African Xoo strains are phylogenetically distinct and use distinct TALes to target SWEETs (Oliva et al., 2019; Tran et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Oliva et al., 2019 and Tran et al., 2018.

claim: African Xoo strains exclusively use TalC and TalF, which both target SWEET14.
source: African Xoo strains exclusively use TalC and TalF, which both target SWEET14, while Asian strains encode PthXo1, PthXo2 (variants A, B, C), PthXo3 and AvrXa7, which target SWEET11a, 13, and 14, respectively (Eom et al., 2019; Oliva et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Eom et al., 2019 and Oliva et al., 2019.

claim: Asian strains encode PthXo1, PthXo2 (variants A, B, C), PthXo3 and AvrXa7, which target SWEET11a, 13, and 14, respectively.
source: African Xoo strains exclusively use TalC and TalF, which both target SWEET14, while Asian strains encode PthXo1, PthXo2 (variants A, B, C), PthXo3 and AvrXa7, which target SWEET11a, 13, and 14, respectively (Eom et al., 2019; Oliva et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Eom et al., 2019 and Oliva et al., 2019.

claim: American Xoo strains lack TALes and hence are poorly virulent.
source: American Xoo strains lack TALes and hence are poorly virulent (Verdier et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Verdier et al., 2012a.

claim: Broad-spectrum resistance to Asian strains was successfully introduced into Oryza sativa ssp. japonica cv. Kitaake and the spp. indica varieties IR64 and Ciherang-Sub1 by genome editing the EBEs in all three SWEET promoters.
source: Based on the information of the TALe compendium and the SWEET target sites, broad-spectrum resistance to Asian strains was successfully introduced into Oryza sativa ssp. japonica cv. Kitaake and the spp. indica varieties IR64 and Ciherang-Sub1 by genome editing the EBEs in all three SWEET promoters (Eom et al., 2019; Oliva et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Eom et al., 2019 and Oliva et al., 2019.

claim: The diagnostic SWEETR kit was developed to enable effective characterization of causative strains and their SWEET-based disease mechanisms.
source: To prepare for emerging strains with novel virulence mechanisms, the diagnostic SWEETR kit was developed, enabling effective characterization of causative strains and their SWEET-based disease mechanisms, and identification of suitable resistance strategies, such as the best possible SWEETR-gene combinations for deployment in the target country (Eom et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Eom et al., 2019.

claim: First observations of BB in Africa were made as early as 1979 in Mali and Cameroon.
source: First observations of BB in Africa were made as early as 1979 in Mali and Cameroon (Buddenhagen et al., 1979).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Buddenhagen et al., 1979.

claim: BB has been reported mostly in West Africa, including Senegal, Benin, Burkina Faso, Ivory Coast, Mali, and Niger.
source: Since then, the disease has been reported mostly in West Africa, including Senegal, Benin, Burkina Faso, Ivory Coast, Mali, and Niger (Afolabi et al., 2016; Gonzalez et al., 2007; Tall et al., 2020; Tekete et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: BB was reported in the East African countries Uganda and Tanzania.
source: More recently, BB was also reported in the East African countries Uganda and Tanzania (Duku et al., 2016; Oliva et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Duku et al., 2016 and Oliva et al., 2019.

claim: In 1975, one of the first irrigated perimeters with rice research labs and a training farm was developed in Dakawa as a result of a multi-year partnership with North Korea.
source: For instance, in 1975, one of the first irrigated perimeters with rice research labs and a training farm was developed in Dakawa, a major rice production zone in Tanzania, as a result of a multi-year partnership with North Korea (van et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to van et al., 2022.

claim: In 2011, a collaboration with China resulted in 50 ha of irrigated fields managed by local farmers in Dakawa.
source: In 2011, a collaboration with China resulted in 50 ha of irrigated fields managed by local farmers.
evidence: This is a historical statement about agricultural development in Tanzania.

claim: A Technology Demonstration Center that trains local farmers and technicians and grows Chinese varieties, including hybrid rice has been established in Dakawa.
source: A Technology Demonstration Center that trains local farmers and technicians and grows Chinese varieties, including hybrid rice has been established (Makundi, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Makundi, 2017.

claim: Disease surveys in Tanzania identified an outbreak of BB in 2019 that has spread in subsequent years.
source: Recent disease surveys in Tanzania, described here, identified an outbreak of BB in 2019 that has spread in subsequent years.
evidence: This is based on field surveys and sampling described in the manuscript.

claim: The causative strains from Tanzania have features that distinguish them from endemic African Xoo strains.
source: We show that the causative strains have features that distinguish them from endemic African Xoo strains, and unravelled the virulence mechanisms that make them a major threat to African rice production.
evidence: This is based on genomic and phenotypic characterization presented in the manuscript.

claim: Kenya and Nigeria exempted SDN-1 genome-edited crops generated using site-directed nuclease without a transgene from GMO regulations.
source: Recently, Kenya and Nigeria exempted SDN-1 genome-edited crops generated using site-directed nuclease without a transgene (SDN-1) from GMO regulations (Buchholzer and Frommer, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Buchholzer and Frommer, 2023.

claim: Komboka (IRO5N-221) is a relatively new high-yielding, semi-aromatic rice variety jointly developed by IRRI and KALRO.
source: Komboka (IRO5N-221) is a relatively new high-yielding, semi-aromatic rice variety jointly developed by IRRI (International Rice Research Institute) and KALRO (Kenya Agricultural & Livestock Research Organization; BBSRC Varieties Kenya.pdf) that grows to an average height of 110cm and has a yield potential of~7 tons/ha, - almost twice that of Basmati, another popular variety planted in Kenya and Rwanda (The Star 2020).
evidence: This is a description of the Komboka variety with references to institutional sources.

claim: Komboka plants mature in~115days.
source: Komboka plants mature in~115days, respond well to fertilization, and are suitable for irrigated lowland cultivation in Africa (Kitilu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kitilu et al., 2019.

claim: Komboka had been classified as moderately resistant to BB, RYMV, and RB.
source: Komboka had been classified as moderately resistant to BB, RYMV, and RB; however, detailed resistance profiles for specific strains or races are not available, rendering this information of little value for breeding resistance in the context of specific pathovars present locally.
evidence: This is a statement about previous classification of Komboka resistance.

claim: BB was not considered a major disease in Tanzania due to low incidence and low severity up until 2019.
source: Local breeders reported that although BB was found in Tanzania, it was not considered a major disease due to low incidence and low severity up until 2019 (RM, pers. comm.).
evidence: This is based on personal communication with local breeders.

claim: An unprecedented BB outbreak was identified in the irrigated schemes of Dakawa and Lukenge in 2019 and 2021, respectively.
source: Here, we report on an unprecedented BB outbreak identified in the irrigated schemes of Dakawa and Lukenge in 2019 and 2021, respectively (Figure 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on field surveys and is illustrated in Figure 1 and supplements.

claim: Dakawa and Lukenge are ~60 km apart in the Morogoro region.
source: The two sites are ~60 km apart in the Morogoro region, an area that for decades has been a center of partnership initiatives that aim at increasing rice production (Makundi, 2017).
evidence: This is a geographical statement supported by a citation.

claim: A severe outbreak was detected in Dakawa on TXD 306 (SARO-5) in 2019.
source: We performed disease surveys in this area in 2019 and detected a severe outbreak in Dakawa on TXD 306 (SARO-5), a rice variety popular in irrigated ecologies in Tanzania (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on field surveys and is illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In 2021 in Lukenge, several fields showed severe signs of infections.
source: Later on, in 2021 in Lukenge, several fields also showed severe signs of infections (Figure 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on field surveys and is illustrated in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Seven strains were isolated from Dakawa in 2019.
source: Leaves collected in 2019 and 2021 with typical BB symptoms were processed, resulting in the isolation of seven strains from Dakawa and 106 from Lukenge, all validated as Xoo using diagnostic primers (Lang et al., 2010; Table 1, Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is based on bacterial isolation and molecular validation.

claim: 106 strains were isolated from Lukenge in 2021.
source: Leaves collected in 2019 and 2021 with typical BB symptoms were processed, resulting in the isolation of seven strains from Dakawa and 106 from Lukenge, all validated as Xoo using diagnostic primers (Lang et al., 2010; Table 1, Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is based on bacterial isolation and molecular validation.

claim: In 2022, over 600 leaf samples were collected from plants with typical BB symptoms from 37 fields in six different regions in Tanzania.
source: In 2022, we surveyed BB on a larger scale and collected over 600 leaf samples from plants with typical BB symptoms from 37 fields in six different regions in Tanzania.
evidence: This is based on field surveys conducted in 2022.

claim: BB has spread across Tanzania.
source: The results of the survey show that BB has spread across Tanzania (Figure 1; Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is based on survey results illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The yield loss in one severely infected field in Dakawa in 2019 was estimated to be >60%.
source: Out of six fields surveyed in Dakawa in 2019, one was very severely infected (Figure 1—figure supplement 1). The yield loss in this field was estimated to be >60%.
evidence: This is an estimate based on field observations.

claim: One of the fields surveyed in Lukenge in 2021 had an estimated yield loss of 10–15%.
source: One of the fields surveyed in Lukenge in 2021 had an estimated yield loss of 10–15%.
evidence: This is an estimate based on field observations.

claim: In 2022, several Dakawa fields had estimated yield losses of 5–10%, others <5%.
source: In 2022, several Dakawa fields had estimated yield losses of 5–10%, others <5%.
evidence: This is an estimate based on field observations.

claim: Yield loss at Igunga was estimated to 10%.
source: Yield loss at other sites such as Igunga was estimated to 10%, in Mombo <5%.
evidence: This is an estimate based on field observations.

claim: Yield loss at Mombo was estimated to <5%.
source: Yield loss at other sites such as Igunga was estimated to 10%, in Mombo <5%.
evidence: This is an estimate based on field observations.

claim: NILs harboring Xa1, Xa23, xa5 or Xa4 were resistant to most endemic African strains.
source: NILs harboring Xa1, Xa23, xa5 or Xa4 were resistant to most endemic African strains, but surprisingly, iTzDak19-1, iTzDak19-2, and iTzDak19-3 were virulent on all NILs tested, except IRBB23.
evidence: This is based on leaf-clipping inoculation assays presented in Table 1.

claim: iTzDak19-1, iTzDak19-2, and iTzDak19-3 were virulent on all NILs tested, except IRBB23.
source: NILs harboring Xa1, Xa23, xa5 or Xa4 were resistant to most endemic African strains, but surprisingly, iTzDak19-1, iTzDak19-2, and iTzDak19-3 were virulent on all NILs tested, except IRBB23.
evidence: This is based on leaf-clipping inoculation assays presented in Table 1.

claim: Most African strains were avirulent on Komboka.
source: Using our African Xoo diversity panel, we found that most African strains were avirulent on Komboka, except for representatives of newly isolated strains from Dakawa (2019) and Lukenge (2021); (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Table 1).
evidence: This is based on leaf-clipping inoculation assays presented in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: Representatives of newly isolated strains from Dakawa (2019) and Lukenge (2021) were virulent on Komboka.
source: Using our African Xoo diversity panel, we found that most African strains were avirulent on Komboka, except for representatives of newly isolated strains from Dakawa (2019) and Lukenge (2021); (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Table 1).
evidence: This is based on leaf-clipping inoculation assays presented in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: All strains were highly virulent on the susceptible variety Azucena.
source: By comparison, all strains were highly virulent on the susceptible variety Azucena (Figure 2—figure supplement 2; Table 1).
evidence: This is based on leaf-clipping inoculation assays presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Table 1.

claim: Komboka contains genetic markers linked to Xa4.
source: Mining of the IRRI QTL database (https://rbi.irri.org/resources-and-tools/qtl-profiles) revealed that Komboka contains genetic markers linked to Xa4 but not xa5 or Xa23, while there was no information on Xa1 in the database (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is based on database mining and is illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Komboka does not contain genetic markers linked to xa5 or Xa23.
source: Mining of the IRRI QTL database (https://rbi.irri.org/resources-and-tools/qtl-profiles) revealed that Komboka contains genetic markers linked to Xa4 but not xa5 or Xa23, while there was no information on Xa1 in the database (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is based on database mining and is illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The presence of Xa4 in Komboka was confirmed by tracing an Xa4-associated marker and by sequencing.
source: We confirmed the presence of Xa4 in Komboka by tracing an Xa4-associated marker and by sequencing (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B,C; Supplementary file 1c).
evidence: This is based on molecular marker analysis and sequencing presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B,C.

claim: Komboka carries a dominant Xa1 allele that is highly similar to Xa45(t).
source: Consistent with the broad-spectrum resistance of Xa1 against endemic African Xoo strains, we found that Komboka carries a dominant Xa1 allele that is highly similar to Xa45(t) (Ji et al., 2020; Figure 2—figure supplement 3D, E).
evidence: This is based on sequencing and phylogenetic analysis presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 3D, E, with a citation to Ji et al., 2020.

claim: The combination of Xa4 and Xa45(t) in Komboka likely can explain the observed resistance to most African Xoo strains.
source: The combination of Xa4 and Xa45(t) in Komboka liekly can explain the observed resistance to most African Xoo strains.
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of these R genes and the resistance phenotype.

claim: The R genes present in Komboka do not protect against the iTz strains recently isolated from the outbreak in Tanzania.
source: However, the R genes present in Komboka do not protect against the iTz strains recently isolated from the outbreak in Tanzania.
evidence: This is based on infection assays showing susceptibility of Komboka to iTz strains.

claim: All eight recently isolated Tanzanian strains clustered with Asian rather than African Xoo isolates.
source: Notably, all eight strains clustered with Asian rather than African Xoo isolates (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on whole-genome SNP-based phylogenetic analysis presented in Figure 3A.

claim: Older Tanzanian strains TzDak11-1, TzDak11-2 and TzDak18-1 grouped with the endemic African lineage.
source: By contrast, older Tanzanian strains TzDak11-1, TzDak11-2 and TzDak18-1, which had been collected in Dakawa before 2019, grouped with the endemic African lineage, consistent with previous reports (Oliva et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis with a citation to Oliva et al., 2019.

claim: The eight recently isolated strains carried only 1–4 core genome SNPs.
source: Based on the analysis of the core genome, the eight recently isolated strains carried only 1–4 core genome SNPs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), intimating that they derive from a single introduction event.
evidence: This is based on core genome SNP analysis presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The eight recently isolated Tanzanian strains derive from a single introduction event.
source: Based on the analysis of the core genome, the eight recently isolated strains carried only 1–4 core genome SNPs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), intimating that they derive from a single introduction event.
evidence: This is an inference based on the low number of SNPs between strains.

claim: The phylogenetic analysis indicates that the new strains (iTz) are most closely related to strains from Yunnan province, China.
source: The phylogenetic analysis indicates that the new strains (named iTz; 'i' for introduced; Tz for Tanzania); are most closely related to strains from Yunnan province, China.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis presented in Figure 3B.

claim: The new Tanzanian strains all carry iTALe genes similar to tal3a of PXO99A.
source: The new strains all carry iTALe genes similar to tal3a of PXO99A (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on genomic sequencing and TALe prediction presented in Figure 3C.

claim: iTALe genes encode truncated TALes that suppress Xa1 resistance.
source: iTALe genes encode truncated TALes that suppress Xa1 resistance, but had so far only been reported in Asian Xoo isolates.
evidence: This is established knowledge about iTALe function.

claim: The new Tanzanian strains contain a TALe (named PthXo1B) highly similar to the Asian PthXo1, with the addition of two RVDs at the N-terminus of the repeat array.
source: In addition, the strains contain a TALe (named PthXo1B) highly similar to the Asian PthXo1, with the addition of two RVDs at the N-terminus of the repeat array (Figure 3D; Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: This is based on genomic sequencing and TALe prediction presented in Figure 3D.

claim: PthXo1B can bind to the SWEET11a promoter at a site overlapping with the EBE that is targeted by PthXo1.
source: EBE prediction indicated that PthXo1B can bind to the SWEET11a promoter at a site overlapping with the EBE that is targeted by PthXo1 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on computational EBE prediction presented in Figure 3D.

claim: ossweet11a knock-out mutants from the diagnostic SWEETR kit were resistant to representative strains from the outbreak in Dakawa and Lukenge.
source: Consistent with a SWEET11a-based susceptibility, ossweet11a knock-out mutants from the diagnostic SWEETR kit were resistant to representative strains from the outbreak in Dakawa and Lukenge, iTzDak19-1 and iTzLuk21-3, whereas ossweet13 or ossweet14 knock-out mutants remained susceptible (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on infection assays using SWEETR kit lines presented in Figure 4A.

claim: ossweet13 or ossweet14 knock-out mutants remained susceptible to iTzDak19-1 and iTzLuk21-3.
source: Consistent with a SWEET11a-based susceptibility, ossweet11a knock-out mutants from the diagnostic SWEETR kit were resistant to representative strains from the outbreak in Dakawa and Lukenge, iTzDak19-1 and iTzLuk21-3, whereas ossweet13 or ossweet14 knock-out mutants remained susceptible (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on infection assays using SWEETR kit lines presented in Figure 4A.

claim: SWEET11a mRNA levels were elevated in Kitaake leaves after inoculation with iTzDak19-1 and iTzLuk21-3.
source: Moreover, SWEET11a mRNA levels were elevated in Kitaake leaves after inoculation with iTzDak19-1 and iTzLuk21-3 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on qRT-PCR analysis presented in Figure 4B.

claim: The iTz strains collected in 2019–2021 in the Morogoro region are >99.99% identical to each other.
source: Together, our data show that the iTz strains collected in 2019–2021 in the Morogoro region are >99.99% identical to each other, and phylogenetically related to Asian Xoo strains.
evidence: This is based on core genome SNP analysis.

claim: The iTz strains are phylogenetically related to Asian Xoo strains.
source: Together, our data show that the iTz strains collected in 2019–2021 in the Morogoro region are >99.99% identical to each other, and phylogenetically related to Asian Xoo strains.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The promoters of SWEET11a, 13 and 14 in Komboka contain EBEs for PthXo1 and PthXo1A, PthXo2A, PthXo3, AvrXa7, TalC, and TalF, respectively.
source: The promoters contain EBEs for PthXo1 and PthXo1A, PthXo2A, PthXo3, AvrXa7, TalC, and TalF, respectively (Figure 5; Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: This is based on sequencing of SWEET promoters and EBE identification presented in Figure 5 and supplements.

claim: All six known EBEs in the promoters of SWEET11a, 13 and 14 were edited using a hybrid Cas9/Cpf1 editing system.
source: To protect Komboka against endemic strains from Africa as well as introduced Asian strains, all six known EBEs in the promoters of SWEET11a, 13 and 14 were edited using a hybrid Cas9/Cpf1 editing system.
evidence: This is based on the genome editing approach described in the manuscript.

claim: Cas9 preferentially produces SNPs due to blunt cleavage.
source: Due to blunt cleavage, Cas9 preferentially produces SNPs, while Cpf1 (Cas12) produces staggered cuts, creating predominantly small deletions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the different cleavage mechanisms of Cas9 and Cpf1.

claim: Cpf1 (Cas12) produces staggered cuts, creating predominantly small deletions.
source: Due to blunt cleavage, Cas9 preferentially produces SNPs, while Cpf1 (Cas12) produces staggered cuts, creating predominantly small deletions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the cleavage mechanism of Cpf1.

claim: Two CRISPR/Cpf1 gRNAs (cXo1 and cXo2) were designed to target PthXo1 /PthXo1 A and PthXo2A EBEs in SWEET11a and SWEET13, respectively.
source: Two CRISPR/Cpf1 gRNAs (cXo1 and cXo2) were designed to target PthXo1 /PthXo1 A and PthXo2A EBEs in SWEET11a and SWEET13, respectively (Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2; Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: This is based on the gRNA design described in the manuscript and illustrated in Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: One CRISPR-Cpf1 gRNA (cTalF) was designed to target the overlapping region of AvrXa7, PthXo3 and TalF EBEs in SWEET14.
source: Since the EBEs for AvrXa7, PthXo3 and TalF in SWEET14 are overlapping, one CRISPR-Cpf1 gRNA (cTalF) was designed to target the overlapping region of all three EBEs.
evidence: This is based on the gRNA design described in the manuscript.

claim: A Cas9 gRNA (gTalC) was designed to target the TalC EBE.
source: Because no TTTV PAM sequence was available near the EBE for TalC for designing a gRNA required by Cpf1, a Cas9 gRNA (gTalC) was designed to target the TalC EBE.
evidence: This is based on the gRNA design described in the manuscript.

claim: Six representative T2 lines were tested for resistance using six representative Xoo strains.
source: From a first round of transformation, six representative T2 lines were tested for resistance using six representative Xoo strains: ME2 (PXO99A mutant deficient in PthXo1), PXO99A (PthXo1), PXO61 (PthXo2B, PthXo3), PXO86 (AvrXa7), MAI1 (TalC, TalF), and BAI3 (TalC) (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 1g-k).
evidence: This is based on infection assays presented in Figure 5A and supplements.

claim: All six lines from the first round of transformation were resistant to the tested strains.
source: All six lines from this first round of transformation were resistant to the tested strains.
evidence: This is based on infection assays presented in Figure 5A.

claim: Line 1.5_19 was fully resistant to all strains tested.
source: One line (1.5_19) was fully resistant to all strains, while five lines were fully resistant to five strains, but only moderately resistant to PXO86.
evidence: This is based on infection assays presented in Figure 5A.

claim: Five lines were fully resistant to five strains, but only moderately resistant to PXO86.
source: One line (1.5_19) was fully resistant to all strains, while five lines were fully resistant to five strains, but only moderately resistant to PXO86.
evidence: This is based on infection assays presented in Figure 5A.

claim: The difference in resistance to PXO86 is most likely explained by the presence of a rather small 4 bp deletion in the EBE for AvrXa7.
source: This difference in resistance is most likely explained by the presence of a rather small 4 bp deletion in the EBE for AvrXa7, while line 1.5_19 carried the same 4 bp deletion plus an additional base pair substitution (G/T) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the mutation analysis presented in Figure 5B.

claim: Line 1.5_19 carried a 4 bp deletion plus an additional base pair substitution (G/T) in the EBE for AvrXa7.
source: This difference in resistance is most likely explained by the presence of a rather small 4 bp deletion in the EBE for AvrXa7, while line 1.5_19 carried the same 4 bp deletion plus an additional base pair substitution (G/T) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on sequencing analysis presented in Figure 5B.

claim: Moderate resistance in clipping assays is generally assumed to be sufficient for effective resistance in field conditions.
source: Since the clipping assays us very high bacterial titers, it is generally assumed that moderate resistance will be sufficient for effective resistance in field conditions (Adhikari et al., 1995; Fred et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Adhikari et al., 1995 and Fred et al., 2016.

claim: TALes were reported to have less specific nucleotide binding at the 3'-end.
source: However, TALes were reported to have less specific nucleotide binding at the 3'-end, hence the G/T substitution in line 1.5_19 could potentially be overcome by adaptation of AvrXa7 (Richter et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Richter et al., 2014.

claim: Two T2 lines (14_19 and 14_65) contained deletions in all EBEs, including 11- and 5 bp deletions in the AvrXa7 EBE, respectively.
source: Two T2 lines (14_19 and 14_65), which contained deletions in all EBEs, including 11- and 5 bp deletions in the AvrXa7 EBE, respectively, were resistant to all strains tested, including PXO86 (Figure 6).
evidence: This is based on sequencing and infection assays presented in Figure 6.

claim: Lines 14_19 and 14_65 were resistant to all strains tested, including PXO86.
source: Two T2 lines (14_19 and 14_65), which contained deletions in all EBEs, including 11- and 5 bp deletions in the AvrXa7 EBE, respectively, were resistant to all strains tested, including PXO86 (Figure 6).
evidence: This is based on infection assays presented in Figure 6.

claim: Lines 1.5_19 and 1.2_40 were resistant to iTzDak19-1 and iTzLuk21-3.
source: Lines 1.5_19 and 1.2_40 were also resistant to iTzDak19-1 and iTzLuk21-3, consistent with the 12- and 9 bp deletions in the predicted PthXo1 EBE (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on infection assays presented in Figure 7.

claim: Induction of SWEET11a by iTzDak19-1 and iTzLuk21-3 was abolished in lines 1.2_40 and 1.5_19.
source: As one may have predicted, induction of SWEET11a by iTzDak19-1 and iTzLuk21-3 was abolished in lines 1.2_40 and 1.5_19 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on qRT-PCR analysis presented in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Komboka lines with full resistance to representative Asian and African Xoo strains were obtained.
source: Taken together, Komboka lines with full resistance to representative Asian and African Xoo strains were obtained; notably with resistance to two representative strains from the emerging iTz population from Dakawa and Lukenge.
evidence: This is a summary of the resistance phenotypes observed in infection assays.

claim: The causative strains from Tanzania are most similar to Asian strains from Yunnan province in China.
source: Through genetic and genomic characterization, the outbreak can be ascribed to a recent colonization event by Xoo strains in the Morogoro region that are most similar to Asian strains, that is, from Yunnan province in China.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Strains that originated from Asia and Africa before 2019 form distinct phylogenetical groups.
source: Notably, strains that originated from Asia and Africa before 2019 form distinct phylogenetical groups (Lang et al., 2019; Tran et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lang et al., 2019 and Tran et al., 2018.

claim: Before 2019, BB incidence was relatively low in Tanzania, and only three strains were isolated between 2011 and 2018.
source: Before 2019, BB incidence was relatively low, and only three strains were isolated between 2011 and 2018 (Oliva et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Oliva et al., 2019.

claim: The three endemic Tanzanian strains cluster with other African Xoo strains based on SNP-based core genome phylogeny analyses.
source: As shown previously, these three endemic Tanzanian strains cluster with other African Xoo strains, mostly from West Africa, based on SNP-based core genome phylogeny analyses, and all African strains make use of TalC as the major virulence TALe, some additionally use TalF to trigger SWEET14 induction (Oliva et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Oliva et al., 2019.

claim: All African strains make use of TalC as the major virulence TALe.
source: As shown previously, these three endemic Tanzanian strains cluster with other African Xoo strains, mostly from West Africa, based on SNP-based core genome phylogeny analyses, and all African strains make use of TalC as the major virulence TALe, some additionally use TalF to trigger SWEET14 induction (Oliva et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Oliva et al., 2019.

claim: Some African strains additionally use TalF to trigger SWEET14 induction.
source: As shown previously, these three endemic Tanzanian strains cluster with other African Xoo strains, mostly from West Africa, based on SNP-based core genome phylogeny analyses, and all African strains make use of TalC as the major virulence TALe, some additionally use TalF to trigger SWEET14 induction (Oliva et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Oliva et al., 2019.

claim: Xoo can be transmitted by tropical storms.
source: Xoo can be transmitted by tropical storms.
evidence: This is a statement about a potential transmission mechanism.

claim: PXO99A may have been introduced rather recently from Nepal or India to the Philippines.
source: Evidence for transmission within Asian countries has been provided, for example, for PXO99A, which may have been introduced rather recently from Nepal or India to the Philippines.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential origin of PXO99A.

claim: Rather effective continental isolation of Xoo strains had been observed.
source: By contrast, rather effective continental isolation had been observed.
evidence: This is a statement about the historical phylogeography of Xoo.

claim: It is likely that many African rice varieties do not contain suitable R-genes that protect against Asian strains.
source: One may hypothesize that if the new Tanzanian strains had been transmitted by storms from Asia, the strains might be more closely related to strains from India or Indonesia based on the geography (Oliva et al., 2019; Quibod et al., 2016; Tran et al., 2018). Due to the distinct evolutionary trace and the resulting absence of coevolution, it is likely that many African rice varieties do not contain suitable R-genes that protect against Asian strains.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of coevolution between African rice varieties and Asian Xoo strains.

claim: The dominant R-gene Xa23 is effective against the iTz strains.
source: Here we identified the dominant R-gene Xa23 as being effective against the iTz strains.
evidence: This is based on infection assays presented in Table 1.

claim: A combination of Xa21 and xa13 might be able to protect against the iTz strains.
source: Based on the sequence information for the iTz strains and resistance profiling of Chinese strains, a combination of Xa21 and xa13 might also be able to protect against the iTz strains.
evidence: This is a speculation based on sequence information and resistance profiling.

claim: Hallmark features of the new strains identified in Tanzania are the presence of iTALes and the PthXo1 homolog PthXo1B.
source: Hallmark features of the new strains identified in Tanzania are the presence of iTALes and the PthXo1 homolog PthXo1B; both are absent from endemic African strains.
evidence: This is based on genomic sequencing and TALe prediction.

claim: iTALes and PthXo1B are absent from endemic African strains.
source: Hallmark features of the new strains identified in Tanzania are the presence of iTALes and the PthXo1 homolog PthXo1B; both are absent from endemic African strains.
evidence: This is based on genomic sequencing and comparison with endemic African strains.

claim: African rice lines carrying Xa1 may be resistant to endemic African strains, but will be susceptible to Asian strains, including those recently introduced to Tanzania.
source: African rice lines carrying Xa1 may thus be resistant to endemic African strains, but will be susceptible to Asian strains, including those recently introduced to Tanzania.
evidence: This is an inference based on the presence of iTALes in Asian strains that suppress Xa1.

claim: Surveys over several years indicate that the outbreak is gaining momentum regarding severity and spread.
source: Surveys over several years, including preliminary data from 2022, indicate that the outbreak is gaining momentum regarding severity and spread, thus potentially becoming a threat to East Africa, and over the course of time, possibly to all of Africa.
evidence: This is based on field surveys conducted over multiple years.

claim: Eight strains from two locations in Morogoro are genetically almost identical, intimating a single introduction event in this region.
source: This study, which so far is based on the full analysis of only a few strains from two locations in Morogoro, shows that eight strains are genetically almost identical, intimating a single introduction event in this region.
evidence: This is based on core genome SNP analysis.

claim: Ectopic induction of at least one clade III SWEET by a TALe is essential for virulence of all Xoo strains characterized to date.
source: We had previously described that ectopic induction of at least one clade III SWEET by a TALe is essential for virulence of all Xoo strains characterized to date (Chen et al., 2012; Eom et al., 2019; Oliva et al., 2019; Streubel et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: A major difference between Asian and African strains is the distinct set of TALes that target SWEETs.
source: A major difference between Asian and African strains is the distinct set of TALes that target SWEETs, in which endemic African strains specifically target only distinct EBEs for TalC and TalF in SWEET14 (Oliva et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Oliva et al., 2019.

claim: It is likely that many African rice varieties contain EBEs in SWEET11a, 13 and 14 promoters that can be targeted by Asian TALes.
source: It is thus likely, due to the absence of coevolution, that many African rice varieties contain EBEs in SWEET11a, 13 and 14 promoters that can be targeted by Asian TALes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of coevolution between African rice varieties and Asian Xoo strains.

claim: In Asia, single R genes and even combinations of several R genes are insufficient for robust resistance.
source: In Asia, single R genes and even combinations of several R genes are insufficient for robust resistance, because new strains evolved that break individual R genes or combinations thereof (Arra et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Arra et al., 2017.

claim: Breeders test current strains against a panel of rice NILs that carry individual, or combinations of different R genes.
source: Therefore, breeders test current strains against a panel of rice NILs that carry individual, or combinations of different R genes (http://www.knowledgebank.irri.org/ricebreedingcourse/Breeding_for_disease_resistance_Blight.htm)(Padmaja et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Padmaja et al., 2017.

claim: Information on the optimal set of R gene combinations is used to stack R genes to obtain the broadest possible spectrum of resistance against local populations of the pathogen.
source: Subsequently information on the optimal set of R gene combinations is used to stack R genes to obtain the broadest possible spectrum of resistance against local populations of the pathogen (Arra et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Arra et al., 2018.

claim: Researchers and breeders use clipping assays with high bacterial titers to evaluate resistance of rice lines to BB.
source: Researchers and breeders use clipping assays with high bacterial titers to evaluate resistance of rice lines to BB (Kauffman et al., 1973).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kauffman et al., 1973.

claim: The clipping assay is considered to be highly predictive of field performance of resistant varieties.
source: The assay, even when performed in greenhouses, is considered to be highly predictive of field performance of resistant varieties (Adhikari et al., 1995; Fred et al., 2016; Padmaja et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: A complete block of induction of SWEET genes by introducing mutations into the EBE is deemed the most effective way to protect rice varieties against the currently known spectrum of Asian and African Xoo strains.
source: Due to the full dependence of Xoo virulence on the activation of particular SWEET genes, a complete block of induction of these SWEET genes by introducing mutations into the EBE is deemed the most effective way to protect rice varieties against the currently known spectrum of Asian and African Xoo strains.
evidence: This is an inference based on the understanding of Xoo virulence mechanisms.

claim: Komboka was chosen for genome editing because it was predicted to become popular in Kenya.
source: Komboka was chosen since it was predicted to become popular in Kenya, a country that established guidelines that allow the use of edited lines, provided they do not contain transgenes (Buchholzer and Frommer, 2023).
evidence: This is a statement about the rationale for choosing Komboka, with a citation to Buchholzer and Frommer, 2023.

claim: Analysis of Komboka showed resistance to endemic African strains due to Xa1 and Xa4.
source: Analysis of Komboka, a high yielding semi-aromatic rice line released in Kenya and Tanzania, showed resistance to endemic African strains due to Xa1 and Xa4.
evidence: This is based on infection assays and R gene analysis.

claim: Both Xa1 and Xa4 had previously been broken in Asia.
source: However, both R-genes had previously been broken in Asia.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the durability of these R genes in Asia.

claim: Komboka was found to be susceptible to Asian strains like PXO99A.
source: Notably, Komboka was found to be susceptible to Asian strains like PXO99A, which carries both iTALes and PthXo1 that suppress Xa1 and induce SWEET11a, respectively.
evidence: This is based on infection assays.

claim: Komboka samples with BB symptoms were found in one district in Tanzania (Mikindani, Mtwara) in 2022.
source: Indeed, we found Komboka samples with BB symptoms in one district in Tanzania (Mikindani, Mtwara, ∼400 km from Dakawa) in 2022.
evidence: This is based on field observations in 2022.

claim: Xa1-mediated resistance has been broken by 95% of the Asian Xoo strains.
source: Xa1-mediated resistance has been broken by 95% of the Asian Xoo strains (Ji et al., 2020), and Xa4-mediated resistance was overcome by the new East African Xoo strains as well as many Asian strains reported previously (Quibod et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ji et al., 2020 and Quibod et al., 2016.

claim: Xa4-mediated resistance was overcome by the new East African Xoo strains as well as many Asian strains reported previously.
source: Xa1-mediated resistance has been broken by 95% of the Asian Xoo strains (Ji et al., 2020), and Xa4-mediated resistance was overcome by the new East African Xoo strains as well as many Asian strains reported previously (Quibod et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Quibod et al., 2016.

claim: Xa1 and Xa4 lack durability due to shifts in the Xoo population or the emergence or introduction of new strains.
source: Thus, Xa1 and Xa4 lack durability due to shifts in the Xoo population or the emergence or introduction of new strains.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that these R genes have been broken.

claim: New lines with broad-spectrum resistance against both Asian and African strains, including the strains found in Tanzania, is required.
source: Thus, new lines with broad-spectrum resistance against both Asian and African strains, including the strains found in Tanzania, is required (Quibod et al., 2020; Vera Cruz et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Quibod et al., 2020 and Vera Cruz et al., 2000.

claim: Editing all known EBEs for both African and Asian SWEET-targeting TALes could be used to engineer full and robust resistance in an emerging elite variety for Africa.
source: We hypothesized that editing all known EBEs for both African and Asian SWEET-targeting TALes could be used to engineer full and robust resistance in an emerging elite variety for Africa.
evidence: This is the hypothesis tested in the manuscript.

claim: Both CRISPR-Cas9 and CRISPR-Cpf1 systems have been widely used in genome editing.
source: Both CRISPR-Cas9 and CRISPR-Cpf1 systems have been widely used in genome editing.
evidence: This is established knowledge about genome editing technologies.

claim: SpCas9 is the first Cas version to offer high editing efficiency across a wide range of plant species.
source: SpCas9 is the first Cas version to offer high editing efficiency across a wide range of plant species.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SpCas9.

claim: LbCpf1 or LbCas12 is another endonuclease which has a lower molecular weight compared to SpCas9 and requires shorter CRISPR RNA (crRNA).
source: LbCpf1 or LbCas12 is another endonuclease which has a lower molecular weight compared to SpCas9 and requires shorter CRISPR RNA (crRNA)(Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2017.

claim: SpCas9 and LbCpf1 both generate double-stranded breaks.
source: SpCas9 and LbCpf1 both generate double-stranded breaks, but Cas9 introduces blunted cuts 3 base pairs upstream of the PAM, while Cpf1 introduces 5 bp staggered cuts downstream of the PAM (Zetsche et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zetsche et al., 2015.

claim: Cas9 introduces blunted cuts 3 base pairs upstream of the PAM.
source: SpCas9 and LbCpf1 both generate double-stranded breaks, but Cas9 introduces blunted cuts 3 base pairs upstream of the PAM, while Cpf1 introduces 5 bp staggered cuts downstream of the PAM (Zetsche et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zetsche et al., 2015.

claim: Cpf1 introduces 5 bp staggered cuts downstream of the PAM.
source: SpCas9 and LbCpf1 both generate double-stranded breaks, but Cas9 introduces blunted cuts 3 base pairs upstream of the PAM, while Cpf1 introduces 5 bp staggered cuts downstream of the PAM (Zetsche et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zetsche et al., 2015.

claim: Cpf1 often produces larger mutations compared to Cas9, which mainly introduces single base pair insertions or deletions (indels).
source: Hence, Cpf1 often produces larger mutations compared to Cas9, which mainly introduces single base pair insertions or deletions (indels).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mutation spectra of Cas9 and Cpf1.

claim: To generate knock-out mutants, single base pair indels in the first exon that result in frameshifts or premature stop codons are sufficient.
source: To generate knock-out mutants, single base pair indels in the first exon that result in frameshifts or premature stop codons are sufficient.
evidence: This is established knowledge about generating knock-out mutants.

claim: To prevent the binding of TALes to their respective EBEs on SWEET promoters, single base pair changes are not always effective due to the degenerate code and the ability to loop out central RVD repeats of the TALes.
source: To prevent the binding of TALes to their respective EBEs on SWEET promoters, single base pair changes are not always effective due to the degenerate code and the ability to loop out central RVD repeats of the TALes (Oliva et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Oliva et al., 2019.

claim: Xoo evolves rapidly and single base pair changes could be overcome quickly, as demonstrated for an xa25-like resistance gene.
source: In addition, Xoo evolves rapidly and, therefore, single base pair changes could be overcome quickly, as demonstrated for an xa25-like resistance gene (Xu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Xu et al., 2019.

claim: Prevention of TALe binding to EBEs depends not only on the number of deleted or inserted base pairs but also on the position of the introduced mutations within the EBE.
source: In addition, prevention of TALe binding to EBEs depends not only on the number of deleted or inserted base pairs but also on the position of the introduced mutations within the EBE.
evidence: This is an inference based on the understanding of TALe-DNA binding.

claim: The RVDs at the 3´-end of TALes, such as N* and NS, have less specificity in nucleotide binding.
source: Especially, the RVDs at the 3´-end of TALes, such as N* and NS, have less specificity in nucleotide binding, therefore, mismatches at the 3´-end of an EBE can be tolerated by the RVDs (Richter et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Richter et al., 2014.

claim: The 1 bp deletion at the 5´-end of the TalC binding site is sufficient for resistance.
source: Here, the 1 bp deletion at the 5´-end of the TalC binding site is sufficient for resistance, while a 4 bp deletion at the 3´-end of the AvrXa7 binding site did not prevent binding of AvrXa7 to its EBE, indicating that mutations at the 5´-end of the TALe binding site are more effective than mutations at the 3´-end in preventing the binding of TALes to EBEs.
evidence: This is based on infection assays and mutation analysis.

claim: A 4 bp deletion at the 3´-end of the AvrXa7 binding site did not prevent binding of AvrXa7 to its EBE.
source: Here, the 1 bp deletion at the 5´-end of the TalC binding site is sufficient for resistance, while a 4 bp deletion at the 3´-end of the AvrXa7 binding site did not prevent binding of AvrXa7 to its EBE, indicating that mutations at the 5´-end of the TALe binding site are more effective than mutations at the 3´-end in preventing the binding of TALes to EBEs.
evidence: This is based on infection assays and mutation analysis.

claim: Mutations at the 5´-end of the TALe binding site are more effective than mutations at the 3´-end in preventing the binding of TALes to EBEs.
source: Here, the 1 bp deletion at the 5´-end of the TalC binding site is sufficient for resistance, while a 4 bp deletion at the 3´-end of the AvrXa7 binding site did not prevent binding of AvrXa7 to its EBE, indicating that mutations at the 5´-end of the TALe binding site are more effective than mutations at the 3´-end in preventing the binding of TALes to EBEs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed resistance phenotypes.

claim: Cas9 cleaves target DNA adjacent to a G-rich PAM.
source: Cas9 cleaves target DNA adjacent to a G-rich PAM, while Cpf1 requires a T-rich PAM sequence (Zetsche et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zetsche et al., 2015 and Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: Cpf1 requires a T-rich PAM sequence.
source: Cas9 cleaves target DNA adjacent to a G-rich PAM, while Cpf1 requires a T-rich PAM sequence (Zetsche et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zetsche et al., 2015 and Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: Combining Cas9 and Cpf1 into a single system enables simultaneous editing in both G- and T-rich regions.
source: Therefore, combining Cas9 and Cpf1 into a single system enables simultaneous editing in both G- and T-rich regions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the PAM requirements of Cas9 and Cpf1.

claim: The BB-resistant IR64 and Ciherang-Sub1 lines developed previously for Asia were generated using four gRNAs for SWEET11a, 13 and 14 promoters, but did not target the TalF EBE in SWEET14.
source: The BB-resistant IR64 and Ciherang-Sub1 lines developed previously for Asia were generated using four gRNAs for SWEET11a, 13 and 14 promoters, but did not target the TalF EBE in SWEET14 which is targeted by African strains specifically (Eom et al., 2019; Oliva et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Eom et al., 2019 and Oliva et al., 2019.

claim: The EBE in the SWEET14 promoter for TalF lacked a suitable SpCas9 NGG-PAM recognition sequence.
source: The EBE in the respective promoters for TalF lacked a suitable SpCas9 NGG-PAM recognition sequence.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of gRNA design for Cas9.

claim: By combining Cpf1 and Cas9 into a hybrid CRISPR-Cas9/Cpf1 system, it became possible to design four gRNAs that target all six known EBEs relevant for BB susceptibility.
source: By combining the two enzymes Cpf1 and Cas9 into a hybrid CRISPR-Cas9/Cpf1 system, it became possible to design four gRNAs (three gRNAs for Cpf1, including one for TalF; and one for Cas9 to target TalC, which lacked a suitable PAM sequence for Cpf1) that target all six known EBEs relevant for BB susceptibility.
evidence: This is based on the gRNA design and genome editing approach described in the manuscript.

claim: The combination of CRISPR-Cas9 and Cpf1 gRNAs in a single system increases the flexibility of choosing suitable gRNAs depending on the available PAM recognition sequences and off-target frequency.
source: The combination of CRISPR-Cas9 and Cpf1 gRNAs in a single system increases the flexibility of choosing suitable gRNAs depending on the available PAM recognition sequences and off-target frequency.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of the hybrid system.

claim: An efficient transformation protocol previously established for Komboka was used to edit all known EBEs in three SWEET promoters.
source: An efficient transformation protocol previously established for Komboka was used here to edit all known EBEs in three SWEET promoters (Luu et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Luu et al., 2020.

claim: For four target sites (cXo1, cXo2c, gTalC, cTalF), 15, 27, 16, and 21 variants were generated, respectively using four gRNAs.
source: For four target sites (cXo1, cXo2c, gTalC, cTalF), we generated 15, 27, 16, and 21 variants, respectively using four gRNAs, demonstrating the successful application of the hybrid Cas9/Cpf1 in multiplex genome editing of the rice variety Komboka.
evidence: This is based on sequencing analysis of edited lines.

claim: Each variant represents a distinct R gene.
source: Each variant represents a distinct R gene.
evidence: This is a statement about the nature of the edited alleles.

claim: Edited Komboka lines were shown to be resistant against a set of representative Asian and African Xoo strains, which harbor all known SWEET-inducing TALes.
source: Edited Komboka lines were shown to be resistant against a set of representative Asian and African Xoo strains, which harbor all known SWEET-inducing TALes.
evidence: This is based on infection assays.

claim: It has been suggested that TALes can evolve rapidly to allow adaption to host resistance due to changes in the respective EBEs.
source: It has been suggested that TALes can evolve rapidly to allow adaption to host resistance due to changes in the respective EBEs.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential for TALe evolution.

claim: It is conceivable that the resistance developed here can be broken by the evolution of new TALe variants that recognize elements in the edited SWEET target promoters.
source: It is thus conceivable that the resistance developed here can be broken by the evolution of new TALe variants that recognize elements in the edited SWEET target promoters (Perez-Quintero and Szurek, 2019).
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential for resistance breakdown, with a citation to Perez-Quintero and Szurek, 2019.
